lab_title: VSEPR Theory: Predicting Molecular Geometry in 3D
top_level_objectives: Use Lewis structures to identify bonding pairs and lone pairs around a central atom.
Predict electron-domain geometry from the number of electron domains using VSEPR theory.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry when lone pairs are present.
Explain how lone pairs alter bond angles and produce deviations from ideal geometries.
Compare VSEPR predictions with common molecular examples such as H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, and XeF4.

scenes.scene_name: From Lewis Structure to Electron Domains
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the workflow from a 2D Lewis structure to counting electron domains around a central atom.
key_visuals: A flat Lewis structure panel showing a central atom with attached atoms and lone pairs
Highlighted bonding regions and lone-pair regions around the central atom
A simple counter that groups single, double, and triple bonds as one domain each
student_actions: Tap bonds and lone pairs in example Lewis structures to classify them as electron domains.
Count the total number of electron domains around the central atom before moving to 3D.

scenes.brief_purpose: Show the central VSEPR idea that electron domains spread out to minimize mutual repulsion.
key_visuals: A central atom surrounded by movable glowing electron-domain clouds
Repulsion arrows between domains that shrink as domains move farther apart
A 3D space where domains settle into stable symmetric arrangements
student_actions: Drag electron domains around the central atom and release them to watch them relax into a minimum-repulsion geometry.
Compare crowded and spread-out arrangements by observing changes in repulsion indicators.

scenes.brief_purpose: Build the canonical electron-domain geometries for 2 through 6 domains.
key_visuals: Linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral arrangements displayed as 3D models
Angle labels such as 180°, 120°, 109.5°, 90°, and 120° where appropriate
A side-by-side gallery showing how geometry changes as domain count increases
student_actions: Select a domain count from 2 to 6 and observe the corresponding electron-domain geometry.
Rotate each model and identify its ideal bond angles.

scenes.scene_name: Molecular Geometry When Lone Pairs Are Present
scenes.brief_purpose: Distinguish the invisible electron-domain geometry from the visible molecular shape formed by atoms only.
key_visuals: Electron-domain models with lone pairs shown as translucent lobes and bonded atoms shown as solid spheres
Examples of bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square pyramidal, and square planar shapes
A toggle that hides lone pairs to reveal molecular geometry
student_actions: Convert selected bonding domains into lone pairs and observe how the named molecular shape changes.
Use the lone-pair visibility toggle to compare electron-domain geometry with molecular geometry.

scenes.scene_name: Lone Pair Repulsion and Bond-Angle Deviations
scenes.brief_purpose: Explain why lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs and compress nearby bond angles.
key_visuals: Methane and water models shown side by side
Bond-angle labels showing 109.5° for CH4 and about 104.5° for H2O
Lone-pair clouds on water drawn larger than bonding-pair regions
student_actions: Adjust or reveal lone pairs on a tetrahedral electron-domain framework and observe the H–O–H angle decrease.
Compare ideal tetrahedral angles with measured angles in water and ammonia.

scenes.brief_purpose: Apply the VSEPR workflow to common molecules and compare predictions with observed structures.
key_visuals: Molecular cards for H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, and XeF4
A prediction board for domain count, electron-domain geometry, molecular geometry, and approximate bond angles
3D observed-structure models appearing after each prediction
student_actions: For each molecule, count domains, choose an electron-domain geometry, and select the molecular geometry.
Reveal the observed 3D structure and check whether the VSEPR prediction matches.
